source: Ackerman & Thompson (2017) Meta-Reasoning: Monitoring and control of thinking and reasoning, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 21(8)
finding: Founding framework. Two levels: object-level reasoning and meta-level monitoring that produces feelings of certainty. Control keeps, changes or stops effort. Built on the Nelson and Narens (1990) memory model, extended to reasoning. Monitoring types: Initial Judgment of Solvability, Feeling of Rightness (FOR), Intermediate Confidence, Final Confidence, Feeling of Error, Final Judgment of Solvability.
numbers: Six organising questions (Box 3). Paradigms in Box 2: remote associates, anagrams, Raven matrices, CRT, number bisection, syllogisms.
quote: Meta-Reasoning refers to the processes that monitor the progress of our reasoning and problem-solving activities and regulate the time and effort devoted to them.
limits: A review. Most monitoring-to-control links are shown by correlation. The authors say research on giving up is thin.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for G1: rethink only when a monitored signal is weak. The agent needs a named signal at each stage (before solving, after first answer, during search, at the end).

source: Ackerman & Thompson (2017) review: FOR and the two-response paradigm
finding: Two-response paradigm: give a fast first answer, rate FOR, then reconsider in free time. Strong FOR means short rethinking and few answer changes. Weak FOR means long rethinking and more changes. Validation steps: ask if the answer was the first one that came to mind, use a deadline or load, check that giving a first answer does not alter the final one.
numbers: No sample sizes in the review; it points to refs 13-16 (Thompson 2011, 2013, Thompson and Johnson 2014).
limits: FOR is cue-based, so it tracks fluency, not difficulty. The paradigm gives rethinking time and change rates, not proof of causal control.
agent_relevance: Template for a code-checked gate: score the first answer's confidence, spend extra budget only when it is low. Needs a second signal because FOR can be wrong.

source: Ackerman & Thompson (2017) review: FOR is a poor guide to accuracy, fluency cue
finding: Fluent answers give high FOR and confidence whether right or wrong. Causal test: solutions shown 50 ms after an anagram, equation or remote-associates problem were judged correct more often than ones shown after 150 or 300 ms, regardless of truth. Familiarity inflates confidence. Conflicting answers (CRT) lower FOR and are truly harder. Pronounceable anagrams are harder but judged easier.
numbers: Delay manipulation 50 vs 150 vs 300 ms (cited study, ref 30). Confidence tracks accuracy only partly.
limits: Review of cited studies; numbers not re-derived. Cues can be valid (conflict) or invalid (fluency, familiarity).
agent_relevance: A model's fluency (low perplexity, short time to answer) is the analogue of a fluency cue. Do not use it alone to skip checks (G3). Disagreement between samples is the valid conflict cue.

source: Ackerman & Thompson (2017) review: Diminishing Criterion Model (Ackerman 2014)
finding: People ask for high confidence early, then lower the bar as time passes. Intermediate confidence rises over time. The first intermediate rating predicts total time spent. Final confidence can be as low as 20%, even when an I-don't-know option exists.
numbers: Final confidence as low as 20% (refs 19, 22). Ratings collected every few seconds in the review; every 15 s in the 2014 remote-associates study (per the chapter).
limits: Tested mostly on compound remote associates and similar lab puzzles.
agent_relevance: Models also drift to low-confidence answers when budget runs out. Make the stop threshold explicit and fixed in code. G6 agrees: submit best attempt, do not abstain.

source: Ackerman & Thompson (2017) review: rethinking rarely changes the answer
finding: In two-response studies reasoners often keep their first answer in the second stage. When the final answer is right, it was usually right from the start. This challenges accounts where slow analysis fixes wrong intuitions. Failure to rethink is framed as metacognitive: strong FOR, weak-but-enough FOR (meets the aspiration level), or low priority on accuracy.
numbers: Cites refs 15 and 37; numbers are in the Bago and De Neys (2017) line.
limits: Descriptive. No base rates here.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: extra thinking is not a free fix. Revision pays only when tied to a real failing signal.

source: Ackerman & Thompson (2017) review: overthinking and individual differences
finding: Metacognitive analysis also covers continuing too long. Reasoners gather more information than needed even when they pay for it (Newell and Shanks work). Three causes of premature stopping are listed: strong FOR, FOR weak but above the aspiration level, and low priority on accuracy.
numbers: No single effect size. Cites refs 43-45.
limits: Human overthinking is mostly shown on information-search tasks, not on reasoning accuracy.
agent_relevance: Names both failure modes the agent must guard: stopping too soon and thinking too long. G7: every extra step must pay for itself.

source: Ackerman & Thompson (2017) chapter: Meta-Reasoning, shedding meta-cognitive light on reasoning research
finding: Longer treatment. FOR is produced by fluency and weakened by conflicting answers (Thompson and Johnson 2014) and unfamiliar terms (Markovits 2015). Rethinking time and change probability vary with FOR across simple and complex tasks. Confidence-accuracy correlation is modest on simple tasks and can be zero on hard tasks (Prowse Turner and Thompson 2009; Shynkaruk and Thompson 2006). Reading difficulty of the problem text affects neither judged nor actual difficulty (Meyer 2015; Thompson 2013).
numbers: Ackerman (2014): compound remote associates, intermediate confidence every 15 s. Final confidence at solution fell the longer solving took. With an I-don't-know option people still gave low-confidence answers after long attempts.
limits: A synthesis. Zero confidence-accuracy correlation applies to hard tasks only.
agent_relevance: On hard problems self-rated confidence is least usable. Use external checks there.

source: Thompson (2009) Dual-process theories: a metacognitive perspective (pre-print chapter)
finding: Original argument. Heuristic answers arrive with a strong Feeling of Rightness. FOR is the reasoner's cue to look no further. FOR is analogous to feeling of knowing and feeling of familiarity in memory, and rests on retrieval fluency. Colleagues given the misleading widget problem said the answer had to be 100, and suspected a joke when told it was wrong.
numbers: Anecdote plus review of the fluency literature (Jacoby, Whittlesea, Koriat, Benjamin and Bjork). No new experiment.
limits: Theory chapter with no data of its own. Later papers supplied the data.
agent_relevance: Gives the mechanism behind G1. A wrong answer with a strong feeling gets no scrutiny, so the doubt signal must come from outside the generating pass (a check, or disagreement).

source: Thompson, Prowse Turner & Pennycook (2011) Intuition, reason, and metacognition, Cognitive Psychology 63
finding: Introduced the two-response paradigm and measured FOR on reasoning tasks. Core claim as reported by the 2017 chapter and review: the stronger the FOR of the first answer, the less rethinking time and the lower the chance of changing the answer. Publisher page returned 403, so this is a secondary account.
numbers: Effect sizes and sample sizes not read this session.
limits: Secondary report only. Treat figures as unverified until the paper is read.
agent_relevance: Founding experiment behind G1. Recheck numbers before quoting them in the schema.

source: Frey, Johnson & De Neys (2018) Individual differences in conflict detection during reasoning (QJEP pre-print)
finding: Three studies with confidence and latency as bias-detection measures. Most biased reasoners show detection (lower confidence on conflict problems) but a subgroup does not. Group averages hide this.
numbers: Study 1 base-rate: 232 biased participants. Confidence on wrong conflict items 68.6% vs 79.0% on right no-conflict items, F(1,230)=59.35, p<.0001, partial eta2=.21. Of biased reasoners 66% lowered confidence (mean drop 20.8%), 28.9% raised it (mean +11.7%), 5.2% same. Study 2 conjunction (107 biased): 57.0% detect (mean drop 25.0%), 32.7% reverse (+18%), 10.3% same; group-level drop 8.4%.
limits: Confidence is self-report; response time also used. About a third of biased reasoners show no sign of conflict.
agent_relevance: About 30% of the time a wrong intuition gives zero doubt signal. Signal-only doubt (G1) will miss those errors by design. Add a checker that is not the model's own feeling.

source: Bago & De Neys (2017) Fast logic? Examining the time course assumption of dual process theory, Cognition 158
finding: Four experiments with two responses under instructions only, a 3000 ms deadline, a memory load, and deadline plus load. Reasoners often gave the correct logical answer as the first, fast, confident response even against a conflicting heuristic. Correct final answers were mostly correct from the start.
numbers: Exp 1 N=101, Exp 2 N=104 (deadline missed on 12% of trials). Of final correct conflict answers 74.8% (base-rate) and 87.6% (syllogism) were already correct at first response. Direction of change on conflict items, average over experiments: base-rate stayed correct 32.7%, stayed wrong 56.7%, wrong to right 10.1%; syllogism stayed correct 42.3%, stayed wrong 48.1%.
limits: Two task types only (base-rate, syllogism). Authors checked that initial correct answers were not guessing. Conflicts with the strict default-interventionist view.
agent_relevance: Re-reasoning rarely rescues a wrong first answer (about 10% wrong to right on base-rate). Heavy rethinking has low yield unless it brings new information such as a check result.

source: Raoelison, Thompson & De Neys (2020) The smart intuitor: cognitive capacity predicts intuitive rather than deliberate thinking, Cognition 204
finding: Two studies with the two-response paradigm under time pressure and load, using direction-of-change. Cognitive capacity predicted a correct first intuition more than correction of a wrong one.
numbers: Capacity vs correct intuitive responding overall r=0.44; vs correction tendency r=0.22. One study tested 160 participants (mean age 20.3).
limits: Student samples. Correlational. Capacity is a composite of several tests.
agent_relevance: Better first drafts beat more revision. Put effort into first-pass quality and independent checks, not only revision loops.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT, Nature Computational Science
finding: Tested the GPT family on 150 CRT-style tasks and semantic illusions. Early models gave atypical answers. Mid models (GPT-3 davinci) fell for the intuitive trap more than humans. ChatGPT and GPT-4 mostly escaped, with chain-of-thought in most answers.
numbers: GPT-3 davinci family intuitive-but-wrong 70-90% vs humans 55%. Correct: ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%, humans 38%, davinci-003 5%. Intuitive: ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%. Chain-of-thought in 97% (ChatGPT-3.5) and 85% (GPT-4) of answers. Human pilot: 38% correct in CRT, 64% intuitive in illusions.
limits: Only answers were scored; no FOR or confidence was elicited. New items lower contamination risk but do not remove it.
agent_relevance: A model-side CRT result. Written step-by-step reasoning, not a feeling, removed the trap. Supports writing out steps on hard items.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false formats. For open answers the model scores its own sample with P(True), better when it first sees several of its own samples. P(IK), the probability the model knows the answer before answering, can be trained and partly transfers, but calibration on new tasks is weak.
numbers: 52B model. Accuracy on five sampling tasks rises when only items with P(True) > 0.5 are kept (Figure 1). P(IK) trained on TriviaQA, tested out of distribution; it rises with relevant source text and with hints on GSM8K.
limits: Calibration held in the format where options are shown. P(IK) needs fine-tuning. Out-of-distribution calibration weak.
agent_relevance: LLM analogue of FOR and judgment of solvability. A usable signal exists once calibrated. G5: use as a hint with code-set thresholds, never as proof.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? Confidence elicitation in LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Benchmarked verbalized confidence, sampling consistency and aggregation on five datasets and five LLMs. Models are overconfident when they verbalize confidence. Calibration improves with capability and with human-inspired prompts. Failure prediction stays weak.
numbers: White-box vs black-box methods differ by AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605. Failure prediction AUROC is near 0.5 for verbalized confidence on average even where ECE is cut. GSM8K with GPT-4 (93.6% accuracy) reached ECE 0.064. About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
limits: Black-box API setting. Worst on professional-knowledge tasks (law, ethics).
agent_relevance: Verbalized self-rated confidence is a weak stop signal. Prefer agreement across samples and external tests.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know, Nature Machine Intelligence
finding: Human users overestimate LLM accuracy under default explanations. Longer explanations raised user confidence with no gain in accuracy. Matching explanation wording to the model's internal confidence narrowed the calibration gap and the discrimination gap.
numbers: Multiple-choice and short-answer questions. Mean model accuracy over 350 questions: 55% (GPT-3.5) and 50% (PaLM2) in one set.
limits: Experiments are on human users, not agent-internal. Explanation length acts as a fluency cue.
agent_relevance: Length is a fluency cue for LLM judges too (G5: length-normalise). Keep self-reports short and tied to a number.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: With oracle labels self-correction looks strong. Without them (intrinsic) accuracy drops. Models change right answers to wrong more often than the reverse, because they cannot judge their own reasoning.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 standard, 75.1 after 3 calls, 74.7 after 5; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CSQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0. Oracle: GPT-4 GSM8K 84.3 -> 97.5. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Prompted self-correction without external feedback. Not a claim that trained correction cannot work.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for G2. Rethinking driven by the model's own doubt is harmful (CSQA 75.8 -> 38.1).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings of ACL)
finding: Splits self-correction into mistake finding and correction. Finding is the bottleneck. With the error location given, correction works and lifts scores across five tasks. A small classifier trained on other data finds mistakes better than prompting a large model.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 chain-of-thought traces from PaLM 2. GPT-4 mistake-finding accuracy 52.87 overall in one table row (39.80 and 43.40 in other columns). Traces sampled to hold 15% correct and 85% incorrect answers.
limits: Traces come from PaLM 2; step-level logic tasks.
agent_relevance: Locating the failing step with code, not model opinion, is the payoff. Matches G2 and the revise state.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: o1-like models burn many tokens on trivial questions. Most gain comes from the first solution round. Later rounds add little accuracy and little new strategy. Self-training that trims redundant rounds keeps accuracy.
numbers: For 2 plus 3, o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one answer had 13 solution rounds. In over 92% of cases the first round contained the correct answer; first round under 60% of tokens (QwQ-32B-Preview on ASDIV: 287 tokens, 38.7% of response). Method cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview, accuracy kept.
limits: Math benchmarks only (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME). Needs fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: A stop rule is missing in the model. Add a code-side stop when a first answer passes an independent check (G1, G7).

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: on the underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: The opposite failure. Models switch between lines of thought without finishing any. Wrong answers show more thought switches and more tokens. A decoding penalty on switching tokens (TIP) improves accuracy without fine-tuning.
numbers: Incorrect responses used 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones. Over 70% of incorrect responses contain at least one correct thought; in over 50% of them, over 10% of thoughts are correct. TIP raised QwQ-32B-Preview Pass@4 on AIME2024 from 43.7% to 51.4%.
limits: Open o1-like models (QwQ, DeepSeek-R1 preview and 671B) on MATH500-Hard, GPQA Diamond (198 questions), AIME2024. Gains modest.
agent_relevance: Effort allocation fails in both directions. Do not branch on every doubt; finish a path before switching (G1).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning models know when they're right: probing hidden states for self-verification
finding: A probe on hidden states predicts the correctness of intermediate answers, is well calibrated, and predicts future correctness before the answer is written. Using it for early exit cut tokens with no accuracy loss.
numbers: Expected calibration error below 0.1. R1-Distill-Qwen-32B over 0.9 ROC-AUC on AIME. 24% fewer inference tokens with probe-based early exit.
limits: Needs white-box access and a trained probe. Out-of-distribution transfer weaker than in-distribution.
agent_relevance: Shows a FOR-like signal exists inside models. In a black-box scaffold approximate it with sample agreement and code checks.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic early exit in reasoning models (DEER)
finding: Stop long chain-of-thought early by watching reasoning transition points: ask for a trial answer and exit when the model is confident. No training needed.
numbers: 10 benchmarks, 11 reasoning LLMs. Chain-of-thought length cut 19.1% to 80.1% on average, accuracy up 0.3% to 5.0%.
limits: Confidence is model-internal token probability. Averages hide per-task variation.
agent_relevance: Operational form of when to stop: confidence in a trial answer at a boundary, with the threshold set by code.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses token-level confidence to filter weak reasoning traces during or after generation. Beats plain majority voting and saves tokens.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B on AIME 2025: pass@1 91.8%, cons@512 97.0%, DeepConf@512 99.9%. Online mode cuts generated tokens by up to 84.7%. DeepConf-low keeps the top 10% of traces by confidence, DeepConf-high the top 90%. HMMT25 for GPT-OSS-120B: cons 92.9 vs one DeepConf variant 88.9 (it can lose).
limits: Open models with log-probability access. Selecting on confidence is not neutral.
agent_relevance: Confidence-based stopping and selection works when the signal is real. G4: samples from one model are correlated, so test against plain voting at equal tokens (G7).

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute
finding: Longer reasoning can hurt. Five failure modes: distraction by irrelevant information (Claude models), overfitting to problem framing (OpenAI o-series), drift from sensible priors to spurious features, trouble keeping focus on constraint tracking, and more concerning behaviours with longer reasoning.
numbers: Tasks in four groups: counting with distractors (Misleading Math, Misleading Python), regression with spurious features (Grades Regression), deduction (Zebra Puzzles), and AI-risk tasks. Per-model accuracy slopes not extracted this session.
limits: Tasks were built to show inverse scaling, so this shows existence, not frequency.
agent_relevance: More thinking is not safe by default. Supports a budget cap and a signal-triggered switch (G1, G7).

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive capabilities of LLMs: an exploration in mathematical problem solving
finding: GPT-4 can label math questions with skill names and cluster them. Giving the model the right skill labels as in-context hints improves solving on GSM8K and MATH.
numbers: Skill labels built from GSM8K and MATH training questions. Exact gains not extracted this session.
limits: This is metacognitive knowledge (what skill is needed), not online monitoring.
agent_relevance: Naming the needed skill before solving is a cheap pre-step; compare with plain at equal tokens.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: The same model generates, critiques and rewrites. Raises human and automatic preference across 7 tasks with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
numbers: About 20% absolute average improvement reported; gains largest on dialog, style and text tasks.
limits: Reasoning tasks gain little, and Huang et al. 2024 show losses on math and QA without an oracle. Preferences partly judged by the same model family.
agent_relevance: Refinement helps style, not logic. Use it only where quality is judged by something other than the author.

source: Ball & Richardson (2025) editorial: Metareasoning, theoretical and methodological developments (Journal of Intelligence)
finding: Overview of a 13-paper special issue. The framework grew inside dual-process theory: Type 1 answers with low FOR trigger Type 2. De Neys (2023): two competing intuitions of similar strength can trigger Type 2. Dual-process accounts of CRT are contested (Bago and De Neys 2019; Stupple 2017; Szaszi 2017). Only one study is flagged as a conceptual replication (Mata 2023).
numbers: 13 articles. Examples: Ferreira 2022 four experiments on base-rate problems; Law 2022 giving-up task; Morsanyi and Hamilton 2023 CRT in autism (6-item CRT-Long); Stanovich and Toplak 2023 13-item actively open-minded thinking scale.
limits: Editorial, so no effect sizes. The last 13,700 characters of the page were not read.
agent_relevance: Few straight replications of the FOR result exist. Plan to test our own gate rather than assume it.
